lines.note: Por a meſa completes the previous page’s Ienuo ſuyuru, setting the meal tray. Ienuo aguru introduces removing or raising it; its Portuguese translation continues below.

The gloss offers removing or setting the table. The next example is an honorific meal-tray expression ending in ſuberu. The initial of Ciojenga is C-like in this worn impression; it is retained, although the meal context suggests a gozen-related form. The visible space in por a is restored.
Ru completes ſuberu, with cudaru as its alternative. Aleuantaremſe or tirarẽſe describes the trays being raised or taken away; the second verb continues below with its printed nasal abbreviation.

runs.text: ſe as meſas de diante dalgũa peßoa honrada.

lines.note: Completes the removal of the trays from before an honoured person. Dalgũa and honrada are supported by enlargement, correcting OCR dalgũs and bonrada; the source’s peßoa representation is retained.
Ien acu is zen aku, good and evil, equated with yoxi axi. The scan restores initial I and the a in acu; the repeated Ien at the right begins the example continued on the next row.
Ien acu wo vaqimayuru means discerning good and evil. The Portuguese is printed Dicernir, without the s of modern discernir; that historical form is not silently repaired.
After completing “evil”, the entry gives Ien acuni catamuqu, inclining toward good and evil. Capital I replaces OCR l, and the Portuguese divided word is Incli-narſe, not Inoli-narſe.

runs.text: narſe ao bem, & mal. ¶ Item, Em todo

lines.note: Narſe completes inclining toward good and evil. Item introduces a broader expression meaning “in any case”, which continues on the next row.
The additional gloss is “in any case”, clarified through the Latin contrast fas/nefas, right or wrong. Printed Porfas remains joined; the transcription does not modernize the multilingual expression.
Ienbi here means completeness or perfection, paraphrased mattacu ſonauaru. The Portuguese describes being perfected or finished, with the second verb continued below.
Acabarſe completes the gloss. Zoſacu jenbi tçucamatçutta says that the work or construction has been completed; the source divides the final verb after t without an added hyphen.

Ta completes tçucamatçutta. The Portuguese states that the works were completed; enlargement supports the nasal ending in A cabarãoſe, retaining the conspicuous gap after A. The worn nasal vowel is a reading caveat. Xiqixin begins a new example concerning bodily form.

runs.text: Formarſe o corpo, ou tomar fi-

lines.note: With Xiqixin above, jenbi ſuru describes the body becoming fully formed. The Portuguese explains formation of the body or taking human form, with fi-gura divided across rows.

runs.text: gura de homem no ventre da mãy. ¶ Itẽ,

lines.note: The body takes human form in the mother’s womb. The damaged last word is read mãe, not OCR mão; the nasal mark and surviving letter tops support “mother”, but the worn final letter remains a caveat. Itẽ introduces a further sense.

runs.text: Ter, ou incluir em ſi. Vt,

lines.note: The next sense is possessing or including something within oneself. The printed verb is incluir, not ineluir; Xojenuo jenbi begins an example about possessing the various virtues.

runs.text: Ter todas as virtudes em ſi.

lines.note: Suru completes the Japanese example: having all virtues within oneself. The translation closes this completeness/possession sense of Ienbi.
This Ienbi denotes beauty, explained by yoqu itçucuxixi. The historical Japanese adjective is preserved as printed; Portuguese Fermoſura, not Fermoſara, supplies the matching noun.
The additional sense is the beauty of virtue, not merely physical beauty. The scan again supports Fermoſura, and the final upright S. labels written usage.
Ienbô is defined as the sect or teaching of the Ienxùs, the Zen community. The embedded Japanese-derived name is kept in the spelling and current type visible in the gloss.
Ienbǒ is a quiet house or residence. Its caron contrasts visibly with the preceding Ienbô’s circumflex; these adjacent headwords must not be homogenized.
Ienbu means a complete body or set, here a complete collection of books. The right edge shows li without a hyphen, despite the draft’s li-; the word continues as uros below.
Uros completes liuros, and inteiro stresses the completeness of the set. The short continuation retains the historical u/v spelling.
Ienbut is a former Buddha, paraphrased maye no Fotoqe. The Portuguese uses Fotoque within its explanation and calls this figure ancient; q̃ is the printed abbreviation for the relative conjunction.
Foi primeiro explains that the Buddha came before. It completes the relative clause of the preceding entry rather than supplying a distinct chronological headword.

Ienchô denotes a previous reign or sovereign, explained by Iendaino teivǒ. The scan gives one initial I and teivǒ, correcting the extra OCR l and the vowel in toivǒ; the Portuguese says a former king.
Iendai is an earlier age or world, paraphrased maye no yo. Paſſa continues into paſſado without a visible hyphen, preserving the physical division.
Do completes paſſado. Iendai mimon means something unheard of in previous ages; the Portuguese broadens this to never seen or heard. The small terminal hyphen after vi is visible on enlargement.
Sta completes vista, followed by “nor heard”. The next example starts Iendai mimonno a-, with a- continuing into the word for an evil deed on the following row.
Cuguiǒ completes acuguiǒ, an evil act. The phrase describes unprecedented wickedness; the Portuguese again says never seen or heard, dividing ouuida across rows.
Da completes ouuida. Iendai mimonno cǒmiǒ introduces an unprecedented achievement or distinction, contrasted with the preceding unprecedented evil; Grã begins the intensified Portuguese description.

runs.text: dißima façanha feita na guerra, ou nunca ou-

lines.note: Dißima completes Grãdißima, an extremely great feat performed in war, or one whose like has never been heard. The source’s double-s representation and abbreviated nasal spelling are retained.
Uida completes ouuida, followed by tal: never having heard of such a feat. This closes the extended example under Iendai.

runs.text: Parteleiro onde ſe poem as meſas.

lines.note: Iendana is a shelf for meal trays. The narrow, worn initial is I, not OCR F; Parteleiro is the printed historical Portuguese form and is not replaced by modern prateleiro.
Iendǒ is the good path, yoqi michi, specifically the path of virtue. The moral meaning is established directly by the bilingual gloss.
Iendǒni iru or itaru means entering or reaching the path of virtue. The Latin l introduces the alternative Japanese verb, while ca- begins Portuguese caminho.
Minho completes caminho, closing the translation “enter the path of virtue”. The short continuation is distinct from the following homophonous Iendǒ for a quiet hermitage.
This Iendǒ is a quiet hall or hermitage, xizucana dǒ, not the preceding path of virtue. The initial is I rather than OCR F; both printed carons are retained.
Iendocu denotes virtue or the merit of good action, paraphrased Ienno tocu. The worn headword begins with an upright I, not the OCR’s italic H; mereci- continues below.
Mentos completes merecimentos. Iendocuuo tçumu is accumulating merits or virtues; the scan supports virtude, restoring the r omitted in OCR vitude.
Ajuntar muitos merecimentos, & virtudes translates the accumulation example. The row is entirely Portuguese and closes this entry.
Iengacu is described as the state or condition of the Ienxùs. The embedded Japanese-derived community name is a typeface-review candidate; it is not an ordinary Japanese headword on this row.
Ienguen means good words, yoi cotoba. Iẽ- begins the example with an abbreviation tilde over e; the whole Japanese fragment is upright, correcting the spurious italic ẽ in the draft.
Guenuo faqu completes Iẽguenuo faqu, uttering good words. The Portuguese directly repeats that meaning; the division and abbreviation above are not expanded in the canonical text.

Ienguiô concerns skilful devising, yocu tacumu, here inventing something good. The initial capital I is restored from the scan, replacing OCR ſ; the circumflex remains distinct from the next column’s caron-marked entry.
Sa completes couſa. Ienguiô fôben illustrates skilful or resourceful means; the Portuguese begins an explanation of inventing something in that manner.
The invention is described as good, wise, and skilful. Couſa replaces OCR conſa, and the visible ampersand after ſabia is restored; the final ampersand carries the explanation into the next row.

The final qualification is a suitable occasion or opportunity. The damaged but legible ocaſião replaces OCR ocaſũo; its nasal ending is retained rather than normalized to a different historical spelling.
Ienguiǒ is good conduct, yoqi voconai, glossed as good exercises or practices. Its caron is retained and not assimilated to the adjacent circumflex-marked forms.
The practices are virtuous works. Ienguiǒni vocotaru means neglecting such conduct; initial vo- represents the Japanese vowel sequence in this historical spelling.
The Portuguese renders the example as failing in good exercises and virtues. The entire row closes the conduct entry above.

Ienguiô is good action, Yoqi xiuaza, alternatively jengô. The scan supports g rather than OCR ç in the headword; second-pass enlargement also shows the alternative’s descending j, not i. Both circumflexes are preserved.
Bras completes obras. Ienguiôuo faguemaſu is applying oneself vigorously to good works; the visible capital I replaces OCR ſ. To- begins todas in the Portuguese translation.

runs.text: das as forças em fazer boas obras.

lines.note: The example is explained as putting all one’s strength into doing good works. This is the completion of Por todas as forças, not a new meaning of the noun.
Iengô likewise means good works, literally Ienno xiuaza. The circumflex belongs to this separate headword and is copied independently of neighbouring accents.

runs.text: Iengo. Maye, vxiro. i, Ato ſaqi.

lines.note: Iengo contrasts front and back, maye and vxiro, also ato ſaqi. The initial is capital I, not OCR l; Portuguese Diãte preserves its nasal abbreviation.

runs.text: & de tras, ou antes, & de pois. ¶

lines.note: The pair also means before and after in time. Ien- begins a Japanese example across the line break; its e is upright, not the isolated italic character supplied by OCR.

Together with Ien- above, this means placing guards in front, behind, left, and right. Enlargement shows banuo, “guards + object particle”, not bando: the apparent ascender is damage from the hole above the u. The Portuguese begins “post watchmen everywhere”.
Das completes todas as partes. A second example, Iengouo bǒzuru, is paraphrased with A-toſaqiuo vaſururu across the next boundary, forgetting what is before and behind.
Toſaqiuo vaſururu completes the paraphrase, rendered as losing awareness of oneself. The Portuguese is visibly spaced a cordo and is not silently joined or modernized.

After completing “oneself”, the entry gives not remembering or not knowing front and back, with the same meaning. Voboyezu and the alternative marker l are separate: OCR voboyezuil incorrectly fused them. Idẽ retains its abbreviation.
This Iengon means good words; the apparatus recommends Ienguen. Cotoba corrects OCR coroba, and the editorial Meliùs retains the visible grave rather than the OCR tilde.
Boas palauras is the Portuguese equivalent of the preceding good-words entry. It is a short continuation, not an independent headword.
A separate Iengon concerns virtue or good works, explained by Ien no coto. The scan restores the initial I omitted from the OCR, while preserving the printed spaces in the synonym.
Obras completes the gloss. Ienji Iengonuo naſu means doing good deeds; the second term begins with a visible upright I, not OCR ſ. Fazer begins the matching Portuguese infinitive.
Boas obras completes Fazer: doing good works. This closes the second Iengon entry and its example.

runs.text: Diante, de tras, à mao eſquerda

lines.note: Iengo ſayǔ lists front, back, left, and right. Enlargement supports the worn a and a two-stroke caron over u, correcting OCR ſiyù; the Portuguese lists the first three directions here.

runs.text: & direita, i, Por todas as partes.

lines.note: The right side completes the four-direction list, paraphrased “everywhere”. The printed mao above remains without an added nasal mark.

runs.text: O que vai diante do Rey,

lines.note: Iengu is a forerunner, paraphrased saqibaxiri. The scan does not contain the extra i in OCR Saiqibaxiri; the Portuguese describes someone going ahead of a king.

runs.text: ou outro ſenhor grande fazendo lugar, ou pre-

lines.note: The person may also precede another great lord, making room or preparing the way. Pre- begins preparando on the following row.

runs.text: parando caminho. ¶ Item, per met. To-

lines.note: Parando completes preparando caminho. Item, per met. introduces the figurative extension, and To- starts the Portuguese verb tomase below.

runs.text: maſe por precurſor, ou apoſentador que vai

lines.note: The figurative sense is a precursor or an advance lodging officer who goes ahead. Apoſentador is interpreted by this preparatory function; the sentence continues with diante.
Diante completes the advance officer’s role: going ahead. This short row closes Iengu and its figurative extension.

runs.text: O eſtar como abſorto em extaſi medi-

lines.note: Iengiǒ denotes absorbed meditation, described in the Portuguese as an ecstatic state. The initial is upright I, not OCR ſ; medi- continues as meditando.

Tando completes meditando, followed by the comparison with the practices of the Ienxùs. The community name is embedded within the Portuguese explanation and is marked for optional whole-word typeface review.
Ien-i denotes a rank or degree of virtue, paraphrased Ienno curai. The internal hyphen is a printed lexical separator, not a line-break mark.
Ien-ini itaru means reaching a degree of virtue. The Japanese retains the internal hyphen, while the Portuguese final che continues into chegar without a supplied terminal hyphen.

runs.text: gar a algum grao de virtude.

lines.note: Gar completes chegar: possessing or reaching some degree of virtue. The unaccented grao is copied as printed.

runs.text: Caixas q̃ ſe vſão por dinheiro, ou moe-

lines.note: Ieni is zeni, money in the form of copper cash coins. Caixas here refers to those coins, not storage boxes; q̃ retains the source’s abbreviated conjunction.
Das completes moedas de cobre, copper coins. This material specification resolves the sense of caixas in the previous row.
Ienibaco is a small box for these coins. Here Caixinha really is a container, in contrast with caixas meaning cash coins in the preceding definition.
De cobre completes “these copper coins”. It remains a separate continuation of the small-money-box entry.

runs.text: Buraco por onde ſe enfião as caixas.

lines.note: Ieniguchi is the hole through which coins are threaded. The scan gives enfião and caixas, correcting the missing i in enfão and the mistaken r in cairas.
Ieniguchini tçunagu is stringing the coins through their holes. The Portuguese Enfiar as caixas expresses that action; caixas still denotes the coins rather than boxes.

runs.text: Corda em que enfião as caixas. No

lines.note: Ieninaua is a cord on which cash coins are threaded. No begins a usage comment about its common spoken name, completed on the next row.
The common form is Iennaua. This Japanese name occurs inside the Portuguese statement “in common speech it is called ...”, so it is an appropriate whole-word typeface-review candidate.
Ien-in is a quiet religious chamber, paraphrased xizzucana cague. The initial I and internal hyphen are visible; Portuguese ſella is retained as printed rather than modernized to cela.
Dos Ienxùs identifies the chamber or cell with the Zen community. The Japanese-derived group name is embedded in an otherwise Portuguese continuation.

runs.text: Semente de virtude. i, Obras virtuo-

lines.note: A different Ien-in means a seed or cause of virtue, explained by virtuous works. The source has a lexical hyphen, not the a in OCR Ienain; virtuo- continues below.

runs.text: ſas de que hum hà de receber depois o pago.

lines.note: These are virtuous works for which one will receive a later recompense. The scan reads the joined depois, not OCR de poir; the grave in hà is retained.
Ienje is a previous age or world, saqi no yo. The entry preserves the dictionary’s broad wording without imposing a narrower interpretation such as a particular former lifetime.
Ienjen means former times, maye maye. Capital I corrects OCR l, and the Portuguese reinforces the repeated temporal sense.
Ienjenno gotocu means as in former times. The Portuguese begins “as it was anciently”, with anti-guamente divided between physical rows.
Guamente completes antiguamente, followed by “or in the past”. This closes the temporal Ienjen entry.
Ienjenni is the adverb “gradually”, paraphrased xidai xidaini. The visible d restores Xidai from OCR Xicai, and Pouco replaces Pouro; the translation continues as “little by little”.

A pouco completes Pouco a pouco, “little by little”. The separate upright Ienji. at the far right is the catchword for the next page and has been moved to its own furniture zone rather than left in this body line.
